metric_rationale: In all chosen trial pairs, the first cue (which has the highest validity) strictly discriminates between Option A and Option B. Take The Best (TTB) will deterministically choose the option endorsed by this top cue, ignoring all other cues. In contrast, the Weighted Additive rule (WADD) integrates all cues, and since the sum of the less valid cues often exceeds the top cue in these specific compensatory trials, WADD will frequently choose the option that lacks the top cue. Therefore, the proportion of choices aligning with the top cue will be near 1.0 for TTB, but significantly lower for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic specifically on 'conflict' trials. In these trials (e.g., A=[1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,1]), the single most valid discriminating cue points to one option, but the sum of the less valid cues points to the other. TTB will consistently choose the option favored by the single best cue, resulting in a high metric value. Conversely, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, allowing the numerous lesser cues to outweigh the single best cue, resulting in a low metric value.

To definitively discriminate between WADD and Random Cue, we can examine the within-subject choice consistency on 'easy' trials where one option is supported by 3 cues and the other by 1 (Trials 5, 6, and 9). 

In WADD, the 3v1 cue advantage produces a very large difference in weighted sums. When passed through the softmax function, this pushes the underlying choice probability almost entirely to 1.0. Thus, WADD predicts that subjects will be highly consistent in their choices across repetitions of these trials, with any deviations driven almost exclusively by the uniform lapse rate (epsilon).

In contrast, Random Cue generates choices by probabilistically sampling a single cue on each trial. Even when 3 cues favor Option A, the 1 opposing cue still has a substantial probability (roughly 20-25%) of being sampled. Therefore, Random Cue predicts inherently probabilistic behavior even before any lapse rate is applied, leading to significantly lower choice consistency across repetitions. 

By computing the mean choice consistency (the maximum of the choice proportion for A or B) specifically on these 3v1 trials, we capture a large, stable gap between the theories that minimizes cross-subject variance caused by unobservable cue weights.

Rather than subtracting hard trials (which inflates the between-subject variance of the metric due to the sum of variances), we isolate the absolute accuracy strictly on the 'easiest' trials (Trials 7, 9, and 10) where the objective score difference is large (>= 0.65). Random Cue strictly limits choice probabilities to a linear mixture of the cues, meaning that even on these 'easy' trials, the accuracy remains relatively low (around ~63%). In contrast, WADD uses a softmax function over the score differences, heavily amplifying the choice probability for the better option on these specific trials (predicting ~90% accuracy). This produces a massive gap between the theories' mean predictions while keeping the between-subject variance tightly bounded.

In every trial of the design, Option B has a strictly higher simple tally of positive features than Option A. Consequently, the Equal Weights (Tallying) model will consistently predict choices for Option B, leading to a near-zero proportion of choosing Option A (driven only by lapse rates). In contrast, Probabilistic Cue Selection (Random Cue) evaluates options probabilistically based on cue validities. Because Option A possesses the most valid cues (e.g., cue 1 and cue 2) in many trials, Random Cue will predict a significantly higher proportion of choices for Option A. Thus, the overall proportion of choosing Option A robustly discriminates the two theories.

Tallying bases its decision solely on whether Option A has more positive cues than Option B, entirely ignoring the magnitude of the difference. In Trial 4 (A has 4 cues, B has 1) and Trial 7 (A has 3, B has 2), Tallying strictly prefers A and predicts the exact same probability of choosing A for both trials. Thus, P(A|T4) - P(A|T7) = 0. Similarly, in Trial 1 and Trial 2, Option B has exactly one more cue than A, so Tallying predicts the exact same probability of choosing A for both trials, making P(A|T1) - P(A|T2) = 0. The combined contrast (P(A|T4) - P(A|T7)) + (P(A|T1) - P(A|T2)) is mathematically guaranteed to have an expected value of 0 for Tallying, completely eliminating parameter-driven variance. For Random Cue, however, choices are highly sensitive to cue validities. The cues in T4 strongly favor A compared to T7, and T1 favors A more than T2. This yields an expected value of ~0.34 for Random Cue, creating an extremely large and reliable contrast.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive Model (WADD) on strictly conflicting trials. On these specific trials, one option has fewer positive features but higher total validity, while the other option has more positive features but lower total validity. WADD predicts a preference for the option with higher total validity (resulting in a metric value > 0.5), whereas Tallying predicts a deterministic preference for the option with more features (resulting in a metric value < 0.5).

The metric computes the proportion of choices for Option B on the specific conflict trial (Trial 1). On this trial, Option B has 3 positive cues (the least valid ones) while Option A has 2 positive cues (the most valid ones). Tallying strictly counts the number of cues and therefore deterministically prefers Option B. The Weighted Additive Model (WADD), however, integrates cue validities and generally finds the sum of Option A's highly valid cues to outweigh Option B's less valid cues, preferring Option A. Thus, Tallying predicts a choice proportion for B significantly above 0.5, while WADD predicts a choice proportion below 0.5.
